solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Crew beginning to digest a poem — one by Kipling

parts.note: to crew a vessel is to man it

indicators.note: the beginning of the word digest is its opening letter

parts.note: a lay is a narrative poem or ballad

explanation.surface: A sailor starting to take in some verse by Kipling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'poem' looks like part of the definition, but it supplies LAY; the definition is just 'one by Kipling'.
explanation.definitionFit: Kipling wrote the poem 'Mandalay', set in Burma, later a popular song ('On the Road to Mandalay').

clue.text: Perpetrator of terrible crimes — a soldier, possibly

indicators.note: terrible signals that the word crimes is wrecked into a new order

parts.note: a soldier ant is one kind of ant, so an ant may be a soldier

explanation.surface: Someone guilty of awful offences might be a military man.
explanation.definitionFit: A miscreant is a wrongdoer, someone who commits villainy.

clue.text: Carved toggle teens sported touring our country

indicators.note: the rearranged teens travel round the letters for the country
sported suggests the teens are shown off in a new arrangement

parts.note: the UK is the setter's country, The Times being British

explanation.surface: Teenagers wore a carved fastener while travelling round Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: A netsuke is a small carved Japanese toggle used to secure a pouch to a kimono sash.

clue.text: Naval force represented by rising male artist

indicators.note: in a down clue rising means read from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: Adam, the first man, stands for a male
RA is a Royal Academician, an artist

explanation.surface: A fleet depicted by an up-and-coming male painter.
explanation.definitionFit: An armada is a fleet of warships, most famously the Spanish one of 1588.

clue.text: Striking? Police officers are doing it regularly

definitions.text: Police officers are doing it regularly
definitions.meaning: police routinely take suspects into custody

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both eye-catching and the act of taking people into custody.

clue.text: Podgy head of company introducing partner

indicators.note: the head of the word company is its first letter

parts.note: the company head brings in a partner, and hubby is an informal word for a husband, a marriage partner

explanation.surface: A rather plump company boss brings along their spouse.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean pleasantly plump or rounded in build.

clue.text: Miss Pecksniff, for example, showing wariness about appeal

indicators.note: the wary word goes round the word for appeal

parts.note: chary means cautious, wary
IT is sex appeal, as in the 1927 film 'It'

explanation.surface: A spinster in Dickens is cautious about a plea.
explanation.walkthrough: Charity Pecksniff is a daughter of Seth Pecksniff in Dickens's 'Martin Chuzzlewit'.
explanation.definitionFit: Charity is Miss Pecksniff's first name, an example of a girl's name.

clue.text: Pure evil on the up! Not taken to court about it?

indicators.note: the word for not taken to court goes round the reversed evil

parts.note: unsued means no one has brought a lawsuit

indicators.note: in a down clue going up means read backwards

parts.note: ill can mean evil, as in ill deeds

explanation.surface: Evil is rising: it is pure, yet nobody has prosecuted it?
explanation.definitionFit: Untarnished, unstained, as in a spotless reputation.

clue.text: Attend prison, leaving note for 1950s dropout

parts.note: to attend is to be at

indicators.note: the musical note departs from the word for prison

parts.note: nick is British slang for prison
C is a musical note

explanation.surface: Go to jail without a word to a Fifties drifter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Attend' gives BE AT, two words run together.
explanation.definitionFit: Beatniks were the 1950s bohemian youth movement who rejected conventional society.

clue.text: Way to engage English class

indicators.note: the abbreviation for way holds the letter for English, as gears engage

parts.note: St is the abbreviation for street, a way

explanation.surface: A method for getting English pupils involved in a lesson.
explanation.definitionFit: A set is a group or class, as in a school set of pupils grouped by ability.

clue.text: Old prison mother will inevitably visit, do we hear?

indicators.note: asks whether we hear it, so the phrase is to be said aloud

parts.note: mother is MA, will inevitably is SHALL, visit is SEE: 'Ma shall see'

explanation.surface: Mum is bound to come and see, isn't she?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ma shall see' spoken sounds like the prison's name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Marshalsea was a notorious London debtors' prison, closed in 1842, where Dickens's father was held.

clue.text: Fairly plump soldiers about to take a French course

indicators.note: turning about means the letters for soldiers are read backwards

parts.note: OR stands for Other Ranks, ordinary soldiers
un is French for a
a dish is a course of a meal

explanation.surface: Plumpish troops come round to have a French meal course.
explanation.definitionFit: The suffix -ish softens round, so the word means somewhat rotund or chubby.

clue.text: Detached territory, one with seaside feature spanning lake

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: the seaside feature stretches over and around the letter for lake

parts.note: sand is a feature of the seaside
L is the map abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: A remote territory with a beach that stretches across a lake.
explanation.definitionFit: Figuratively, an isolated enclave cut off from its surroundings, like an island of land in water.

clue.text: Terminates alliances

definitions.meaning: to axe something is to end or cut it, so it terminates
the Axis was the alliance of Germany, Italy and Japan in WWII; plural, alliances

explanation.definitionFit: One word is the verb for cutting or ending, and also the plural of an axis, a political alliance.

clue.text: Draw attention to rebuff outside bank

indicators.note: the snub sits outside, around, the word for bank

parts.note: a slight is a snub or rebuff
a pot is a bank of money, a pool or kitty

explanation.surface: Highlight a snub given outside a bank.
explanation.definitionFit: To spotlight something is to focus public attention on it, as a stage light does.

clue.text: Pirate captain twinkles, entertaining last of many children

indicators.note: to entertain is to take in as a guest, so the captain's name and the twinkles hold a letter

parts.note: Captain William Kidd was a notorious 17th-century pirate
winks, like twinkles, are quick flashes of the eye

indicators.note: the last of the word many is its final letter

explanation.surface: A pirate's eyes sparkle as he amuses a crowd of youngsters.
explanation.definitionFit: A playful British colloquialism for small kids, little ones.

clue.text: Outmanoeuvre Charlie, reluctant washer-up

parts.note: to dish an opponent is to outwit or ruin them
Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet
loth means reluctant or unwilling

explanation.surface: Charlie outwits by not wanting to do the dishes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'washer-up' looks like a person; it is the cloth that does the washing.
explanation.definitionFit: The cloth wipes and cleans plates, so it is a washer of dishes.

clue.text: Carrier starts to ship goods, securing awfully bad deal

indicators.note: the two starting letters hold the rearranged deal fast between them
the starts of the words ship and goods are their first letters
awfully signals the words bad deal are badly rearranged

explanation.surface: A shipper starts to dispatch goods while locking in a dreadful bargain.
explanation.definitionFit: A saddlebag is a bag hung from a saddle for carrying things.

clue.text: Geometrician rejected books, heading off one arguing in defence

indicators.note: thrown back, so the letters for books are read backwards

parts.note: OT is the Old Testament, a set of books of the Bible

indicators.note: the defender's word loses its head, its first letter

parts.note: an apologist argues in defence of a cause

explanation.surface: A mathematician tosses aside the books and decapitates a defender.
explanation.definitionFit: Topology is a branch of geometry, so one who studies it is a kind of geometer.

clue.text: Circles in which literary princess is offered culinary herb

indicators.note: the circles have the princess inside them

parts.note: O is a circle, so two circles are OO
Regan is one of King Lear's daughters, a princess in Shakespeare

explanation.surface: Social circles where a princess from a book is served a herb.
explanation.definitionFit: Oregano is a herb much used in Italian and Greek cooking.

clue.text: Result of the writer supporting public business enterprise

indicators.note: in a down clue the writer's word sits below, holding up the rest

parts.note: out means public, known, as in 'the secret is out'
Co is the abbreviation for company, a business enterprise
the setter refers to themself as me

explanation.surface: The upshot of the author backing a state-owned firm.
explanation.definitionFit: An outcome is the consequence or end result of something.

clue.text: Exploit of daughter on river

indicators.note: in an across clue the daughter's letter sits on, following, the river

parts.note: the Dee is a river in Wales, England and also Scotland

explanation.surface: The exploits of a daughter who lives beside a river.
explanation.definitionFit: An exploit is a feat or notable act, as in brave deeds.

clue.text: High-ranking old Turk's aim visiting parts of Fife

indicators.note: the word for aim goes in among the rearranged letters
the place name is broken into parts and put back together differently

parts.note: an end is an aim or goal

explanation.surface: An Ottoman dignitary's goal of touring regions of Fife, in Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Effendi was a title of respect for a man of standing in the Ottoman Empire.

clue.text: Trying experience of boy turning up during exam

indicators.note: the reversed boy sits inside the exam

parts.note: an oral is a spoken exam

indicators.note: in a down clue turning up means read backwards

parts.note: Ed is a boy's name, short for Edward

explanation.surface: A boy's tough time arriving late for a test.
explanation.definitionFit: An ordeal is a severe trial or painful test of endurance.

clue.text: It may be fired about 45 inches in temper

indicators.note: the measure is placed within the word for temper

parts.note: a pet is a fit of bad temper or sulk
an ell is an old measure of cloth, about 45 inches in England

explanation.surface: Something shot off from roughly four feet away in a rage.
explanation.definitionFit: A small ball of shot is what an air rifle or shotgun fires.

clue.text: Wicked one put out by my sneering?

indicators.note: the letter for one is ejected and its place taken by the exclamation

parts.note: sinful means wicked
I is the Roman numeral for one
'my!' and 'cor!' are both exclamations of surprise

explanation.surface: A wicked person annoyed by my mocking manner?
explanation.walkthrough: COR is British slang for an exclamation of surprise like 'my!'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sneering shows contempt and disdain, so it is a scornful attitude.

clue.text: Limited view initially of girl missing point, hating some Brits

indicators.note: cut short, so the word for view loses its final letter

parts.note: an angle is a point of view, a viewpoint

indicators.note: the initial of the word of is its first letter
the girl's name is lacking the letter for a compass point

parts.note: Phoebe is a girl's name
E is east, a point of the compass

explanation.surface: A narrow outlook, starting with a girl without a point, despising some Britons.
explanation.definitionFit: An Anglophobe dislikes England and the English, some of the people of Britain.

clue.text: Aristocrat using good French in retirement

indicators.note: retiring is drawing back, so the French word is read backwards

parts.note: bon is French for good

explanation.surface: A nobleman who speaks good French after leaving work.
explanation.definitionFit: A nob is British slang for a person of high social rank or wealth.

clue.text: Port Wellington left before onset of engagement

indicators.note: the earlier letters come before the final one

parts.note: a wellington is a rubber boot

indicators.note: the onset of the word engagement is its first letter

explanation.surface: Wellington left a port just before the battle began.
explanation.walkthrough: Bootle is a port town on the Mersey, next to Liverpool.
explanation.definitionFit: Bootle, in Merseyside, is a docks town on the River Mersey.

clue.text: Delaying getting accommodation for books, perhaps

definitions.meaning: to shelve a plan is to postpone it
fitting shelves gives books, among other things, somewhere to sit

explanation.definitionFit: Shelving is both postponing a matter and the set of shelves holding books in a room.
